plain_language_explanation: The health plan denied coverage for Vyepti (eptinezumab-jjmr), an infused medication for preventing chronic migraines. The patient is a woman in her 20s with chronic migraine who is under active neurology care. She currently receives Vyepti infusions as part of a multi-drug preventive regimen that also includes nerve blocks every 6 weeks, zonisamide, gabapentin, and magnesium. The insurer denied Vyepti and instead offered Ajovy, a different migraine preventive drug from the same class (CGRP agents) that the patient would self-inject at home. The denial appears to be based on the plan's formulary preference for Ajovy as the preferred self-administered CGRP therapy, rather than on a determination that Vyepti is not medically necessary.

evidence_checklist.item: Complete plan formulary and medical necessity policy for CGRP inhibitors, specifically showing any step-therapy requirements
Neurology visit notes documenting clinical response to Vyepti (migraine frequency, severity, functional improvement)
Documentation of whether Ajovy was specifically tried, and if so, the outcome; if not tried, clinical justification for why it should not be required
Complete records of Aimovig and Emgality trials, including duration, dosing, adherence, and reasons for discontinuation
Clinical documentation of needle aversion if it rises to a level that would constitute a medical contraindication or barrier to self-injection
Letter of medical necessity from treating neurologist explaining why Vyepti is specifically indicated over self-administered alternatives
Headache diary or other objective tracking of migraine frequency before and after starting Vyepti
Appeal deadline and procedural requirements from plan denial letter or Summary Plan Description

recommended_strategy: Appeal on the basis that the patient has already failed adequate trials of two CGRP inhibitors from the same class (Aimovig and Emgality) and multiple other preventive drug classes, demonstrating refractory chronic migraine that warrants a trial of an infused CGRP agent. Argue that requiring trial of a third self-administered CGRP agent (Ajovy) when two have already failed is unlikely to benefit the patient and delays access to a therapy already deemed appropriate by the treating neurologist. If needle aversion is clinically significant, obtain documentation from the neurologist. If Ajovy has been tried, document that clearly. Request the plan's specific medical necessity criteria and step-therapy protocol for CGRP inhibitors, and argue that the patient meets any reasonable definition of having exhausted self-administered options. Emphasize that Vyepti is already part of the current treatment plan under specialist care, implying clinical appropriateness and potentially observed benefit.
draft_appeal:
To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing to appeal the denial of coverage for Vyepti (eptinezumab-jjmr) infusions for the treatment of my chronic migraine. I am currently under the care of a neurologist for chronic migraine and have been prescribed Vyepti as part of a comprehensive preventive regimen.

I have tried numerous migraine preventive therapies without adequate benefit or due to intolerable side effects:
- Amitriptyline: no benefit
- Propranolol and atenolol: discontinued due to dropping blood pressure
- Aimovig: tried for over 3 months without benefit
- Emgality: tried for 4 months without benefit

My current preventive regimen includes nerve blocks every 6 weeks, zonisamide, gabapentin, magnesium, and Vyepti infusions. I also take duloxetine, levothyroxine, Nexplanon, spironolactone, and hydroxyzine as needed for other conditions. Despite this complex regimen, my migraines remain chronic and require ongoing specialist management.

I understand that the plan has offered Ajovy as an alternative CGRP inhibitor. However, I have already tried two other medications in this same class—Aimovig for over 3 months and Emgality for 4 months—without benefit. Requiring me to try a third self-administered CGRP agent when two have already failed is unlikely to provide relief and only delays access to the treatment my neurologist has determined appropriate for my condition.

Additionally, I have an aversion to needles and self-injection, which may affect my ability to consistently adhere to a self-administered therapy like Ajovy.

My neurologist has prescribed Vyepti infusions as part of my current treatment plan, and I am already receiving this therapy under their supervision. I respectfully request that the plan approve coverage for Vyepti so that I can continue the treatment regimen my specialist has determined is medically necessary for my refractory chronic migraine.

Thank you for reconsidering this denial.

Sincerely,
[Patient Name]

procedural_route.details: The packet identifies this as a New York DFS External Appeal (case number 202202-146311), indicating the patient has already pursued external review in New York. However, the packet does not contain the original denial letter, Summary Plan Description, or plan documents that would specify internal appeal deadlines, external review timelines, or the procedural steps required. The fact that an external appeal decision was reached suggests procedural routes were followed, but I cannot state specific deadlines or next steps from the information provided.

outcome_estimate.reasons: The outcome depends critically on information not in the packet: (1) whether Ajovy was specifically tried; (2) the plan's written step-therapy policy; (3) whether Vyepti has produced documented clinical improvement; and (4) whether needle aversion is medically documented. If Ajovy was not tried and the plan's policy strictly requires it, the appeal faces an uphill battle unless needle aversion or futility of a third CGRP trial can be persuasively argued. If Ajovy was tried and failed, or if the patient has documented improvement on Vyepti, the case is much stronger. The fact that two CGRP agents have already failed supports the argument that the class may not work for this patient via self-injection, but plans often require exhaustion of all formulary-preferred options. Without knowing the plan's specific policy and whether Ajovy was tried, I cannot confidently predict the outcome.
